items.excerpt: ## Here is a select list of stories to start the day Published - October 28, 2026 07:06 am IST The Hindu Bureau ... #### Cyclone Arnab’s landfall process continues along Andhra coast The very severe cyclonic storm ‘Arnab’ has begun its landfall process near Narsapur town in West Godavari district of Andhra Pradesh, at around 1.30 a.m. on Wednesday (October 28, 2026). Experts from the India Meteorological Department (IMD), however, said it is too early to indicate the exact location of the landfall. #### First Israeli election exit polls show narrow edge for Opposition The first exit polls from Israel’s elections showed the opposition bloc with a slight edge over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s camp as voting ended Tuesday (October 27, 2026), but still shy of an outright majority in the 120-seat Knesset. The country’s main pollsters projected the Opposition bloc to win 52 or 53 seats, and Mr. Netanyahu’s bloc to win 50, although his Likud would be the largest single party in the parliament, with 24 or 25 seats. #### 40 FIRs over anti-SIR protests in Delhi; police scan CCTV footage to identify demonstrators Delhi Police has registered at least 40 First Information Reports (FIRs) in connection with the protests against the special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in the national capital since October 10, with teams analysing CCTV footage to identify those involved in the demonstrations, officials told The Hindu. #### Delhi SIR: Over 94% of electors flagged for discrepancies cleared for final electoral roll Of the 33,14,032 electors issued notices over lack of mapping or logical discrepancies in Delhi’s draft electoral roll, 31,26,576 (94.34%) have been cleared for inclusion in the final roll, the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) said on Tuesday. Among the 19,34,243 cases involving logical discrepancies, 98.05% have been disposed of. The remaining cases are expected to be settled shortly, the CEO’s office said. #### Bihar MLC results: BJP win one seat, counting underway on remaining seven National Democratic Alliance (NDA) candidate on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) representing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) Narendra Prasad Singh won the Tirhut teachers constituency seat by defeating independent candidate Bhushan Jha in Bihar Legislative Council polls. Mr. Singh secured 2,945 votes, whereas Mr. Jha received 2,351 votes. ... #### BRICS parliamentary forum expresses ‘deep concern’ about West Asian hostilities Expressing ‘deep concern’ about the escalating tension and hostilities in West Asia, parliamentary leaders from the BRICS nations slammed “unilateral coercive measures” and “unilateral economic sanctions” imposed in the region as contrary to international law. items.excerpt: Published Oct 28, 2026, 06:28 AM Updated Oct 28, 2026, 06:28 AM ## Israeli exit polls show deadlock, setback for Netanyahu Israel’s wartime election appeared deadlocked on Oct 27, exit polls showed, a potential setback for veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu if the projections hold, with neither side having a clear path to power but rival Gadi Eisenkot’s larger bloc potentially giving him the first chance to form a government. The stalemate could yet work in Netanyahu’s favour, allowing the prime minister to remain in power in a caretaker capacity while parties try to forge a governing coalition. Turnout was 77.7%, Israel’s Central Elections Committee said, the highest in more than two decades and around 7 percentage points higher than in the previous election in 2022. Israel’s three major networks updated their exit polls, giving Eisenkot’s bloc a two-seat edge over Netanyahu’s Likud-led camp, at 52-50 respectively. The remaining 18 seats were allocated to unaligned Arab parties in the exit polls. ## Trump will respect US midterm results ‘if they’re honest’ President Donald Trump said on Oct 27 he would respect the results of the US midterm elections “if they’re honest,” in what appeared to be a fresh bid to sow doubt ahead of next week’s crucial vote. Trump has ramped up his baseless, years-old claims of mass voter fraud as polls show Republicans could lose control of Congress in the Nov 3 elections. “I will, if they’re honest elections,” Trump told reporters when asked if he would respect the results of the midterms, as he headed on a campaign trip to Texas. ## Flavio Bolsonaro, family to receive US visas after leaving Brazil PHOTO: BLOOMBERG Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has left the country for the United States after losing the Oct 25 presidential election, three sources said on Oct 27, with the US State Department due to grant him and his family entry visas. Bolsonaro, who has yet to concede to leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, left Brazil after refusing to comply with a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports. The ruling relates to a money laundering probe in which he denies wrongdoing. ## Ukraine, Russia say US-brokered Oleshky truce holding PHOTO: REUTERS A local truce between Ukraine and Russia aimed at allowing humanitarian aid into the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky appeared to be holding on Oct 27, with neither side reporting any violations after several hours. Both sides said they began observing the truce at 3am local time (9am in Singapore). The war-ravaged city in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region had been caught in the middle of fighting between the two sides since 2022, when it was seized by Russian forces at the start of their invasion. ## Pope’s cancer a ‘gamechanger’ for papacy ... Pope Leo’s lung cancer diagnosis and surgery has affected how Catholics view his health and papacy, the Vatican’s foreign minister said on Oct 27. “It’s a bit of a gamechanger,” Archbishop Paul Gallagher told journalists at an event in Rome. Leo, 71, had part of one lung removed in surgery on Oct 13. His doctors have said the cancer was localised and had not spread, and the pope will not require further treatment.

items.title: US business activity cools in October; strong demand fueling price pressures By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - US business activity slowed modestly in October, though robust demand allowed companies to raise prices for goods and services, a sign that inflation could increase further and remain persistently high in the coming months. S&P Global said on Friday its flash US Composite PMI Output Index, which tracks the manufacturing and services sectors, slipped to 57.6 this month from a five-year high reading of 58.4 in September. A reading above 50 indicates expansion in the private sector. Strength in manufacturing was offset by a slight pullback in the vast services sector. The PMI suggested the economy started the fourth quarter on solid footing following what is expected to have been a strong performance in the July-September quarter. Economists expect the government’s advance gross domestic product report next week to show the economy growing at around a 3.0% annualized rate last quarter, mainly driven by consumer spending and business investment in AI. The economy has so far not shown any signs of buckling under the weight of the oil price shock stemming from the US-Israeli war with Iran, with savings, generous tax returns in the spring, tariff refunds, a strong stock market performance and corporate profits providing a cushion. Economists warned that the inflation fallout from the drawn-out Middle East conflict was likely to slow consumer spending this quarter. The survey’s measure of new orders received by businesses edged up to 58.2 this month, the highest level since March 2022, from 58.1 in September. The increase was mostly in the services sector, with S&P Global noting "rising domestic demand, boosted partly by precautionary stock building" and growth in exports. Its gauge of prices for output rose to 59.8, the highest reading since August 2022, from 58.4 in September. Businesses across manufacturing and services sectors raised prices. Delivery performance by suppliers to manufacturers deteriorated further. The survey’s measure of suppliers’ delivery times dropped to a more than four-year low of 38.1 from 40.9 in September. SUPPLY BOTTLENECKS INTENSIFYING "Cost pressures remain a key concern," said Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. "Supply chain bottlenecks have meanwhile intensified, and order book backlogs are growing, making it easier for companies to pass higher costs on to customers."

items.title: Beyond Energy: Inflation Heats Up as Fed Gathers | Charles Schwab
items.excerpt: October 27, 2026• Henry Hoenig ... The Fed's preferred inflation gauge, the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, due October 29, is expected to show that core prices rose 0.34% month over month in September, according to the median forecast in a survey by The Wall Street Journal. That would be the biggest month-over-month increase since January, before the Iran war started. While energy prices accounted for a majority of overall inflation in September, according to the Consumer Price Index (CPI), robust and accelerating price pressures showed up in multiple, heavily weighted non-energy categories, underscoring the risk that inflation could spread beyond oil and gas prices. Core CPI, which excludes energy and food prices, rose 0.3% in September from August, accounting for 44% of the CPI's overall 0.6% month-over-month increase. And it's not just one month. Core inflation has been running hot for several months. Through September, it rose at an annualized rate of 3.4% over the previous three months versus a six-month annualized rate of 2.9%. The Fed's target is 2% inflation as measured by the overall PCE price index. ... As is often the case, services prices were the largest non-energy contributor to inflation in September, according to CPI data, accounting for 38% of the CPI's month-over-month rise. Excluding energy-related services, services prices rose 0.4% from a month earlier and accounted for 37% of overall inflation. The three-month annualized rate hit 3.8%. ... O ... PPI for final demand, the headline index, rose 1.3% from a month earlier, the biggest one-month jump since 2022. Excluding energy, food, and trade services (a gauge of wholesale and retail margins), PPI for final demand rose a robust 0.5% from the previous month. ... That was the biggest one-month increase in goods prices since 2009. Services prices rose 0.8%, the biggest gain since April. Further upstream, at the intermediate-demand stage, price increases were "broad-based," the BLS said.

items.title: US midterms briefing: Trump's campaign swing and Democrats' Texas worries - ABC News
items.excerpt: ## Here's what you need to know today - Trump's Texas blitz: US President Donald Trump is hitting two rally stops in Corpus Christi and Lubbock, Texas, in support of Republican US Senate candidate Ken Paxton. He's set to use the campaign swing to announce a plan to ease methane rules for oil and gas producers. That's part of an effort to show voters he's working to bring down petrol prices. This isn't the first step he has taken on the matter, either. Earlier this month, he struck a deal for the US to buy diesel from Russia. He also signed an executive order to let tax-free, red-dyed off-road diesel be used on public roads, though he told a rally he wasn't sure what that meant. - Texas Democrats biting nails: Democrats hope James Talarico will be the first party candidate to be elected to the Senate in Texas in more than three decades. And while polling suggests Talarico has a narrow lead over Paxton, some party insiders worry Talarico hasn't done enough to turn out Black voters, according to a report by The Washington Sun. "The question is not whether Talarico gets the majority of the Black vote because Talarico is going to get the majority of Black votes," Democratic state representative Jolanda Jones told the Sun. "The question is how many Black people are going to show up to vote." - Election interference preparations: State and local election officials across the US are planning how to respond to a range of potential interference attempts, The New York Times reports. Scenarios include potential Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids, overreach by federal monitors, and ballot theft. This stems from concerns that Trump may try to dispute midterm results, even as he still falsely claims he won the 2020 presidential election. ... Rising prices and living costs are the top voter concerns in most polls. There are several Trump actions tied up in those issues: the war with Iran, tariffs, and his repeated insistence that "affordability" is either a hoax issue or one to blame on Joe Biden. Corruption is also breaking through as a big one — a Fox News poll recently found more voters were concerned about corruption (60 per cent) than inflation (58 per cent). ... Some Republicans in close races are keeping their distance or even speaking out against Trump policies. For example, Senate candidates like Susan Collins (Maine) and Mike Rogers (Michigan) have criticised the tariffs on Canada (which their states border) and called for an end to the Iran war. ... The incumbent president's party almost always loses House seats in midterm elections, and that trend gets steeper when the president is unpopular. Historic polling data collated by analytics firm Gallup shows presidents with approval ratings below 50 per cent have seen their party lose an average of 37 House seats. The federal district judge overseeing the Justice Department's lawsuit asking California to segregate roughly 20,000 ballot belonging to individuals it claims are "likely" noncitizens appeared skeptical of the DOJ's efforts to seek emergency action just a week from the state's election. U.S. District Judge David O. Carter said in court Tuesday he intends to appoint a special master to probe DOJ's process that led it to compile the list of alleged 20,000 likely non-citizens, dealing a setback to the Trump administration's attempt to quickly intervene in the election. Judge Carter did not rule by the conclusion of the hearing on the DOJ request for a temporary restraining order against the state, though he appeared skeptical of the department's late-stage attempt to force what he described as a "monumental change" in California's ongoing administration of its election. ... Carter told the parties he intends to issue some kind of ruling governing proceedings on the case moving forward by tomorrow. Bill Essayli, a controversial Trump-installed leader of the U.S. Attorney's Office in the Central District of California, argued in the hearing that the administration was simply pushing for the state to be in compliance with federal law barring non-citizens from casting votes. But state officials and other legal advocates opposing the DOJ lawsuit countered that the litigation violated longstanding Constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections -- and could have chaotic consequences for the state in tabulating final vote counts in the weeks ahead. Notably in closing out the hearing, Judge Carter appeared to admonish the administration over its recent letters to state officials around California suggesting it could prosecute them if they are involved in tabulating ballots that could be from the list of alleged likely noncitizens. "This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately," Carter said. "Good night." On Monday, a federal appeals court rejected a request from the DOJ to issue an order requiring California to set aside the 20,000 ballots from its list, kicking the back to the district court. Earlier this month, the DOJ filed suit against California, accusing the state of failing to review the list of alleged noncitizens that the Trump administration claimed were sent mail-in ballots for next week's midterm election. In court papers filed earlier last week, Los Angeles officials said a preliminary analysis of 200 of the names on the 20,000-person list, included a "high percentage" of individuals who say they were born in the U.S. and many more who have no voting history at all.

items.title: Republicans fear "red scream" could depress GOP voter turnout
items.excerpt: Senate Republicans see Iowa moving their way and Ohio slipping, with pessimism growing over Alaska and Kansas. Why it matters: Even when they squint, top Republicans struggle to see a majority beyond 51 seats, according to half a dozen senior operatives. - ✈️ A combination of paid media and Air Force One visits has bolstered GOP confidence that they'll hold South Carolina and Mississippi. - But across the map, the outlook looks bleak, with only a few bright spots. Zoom out: Republicans are fighting a two-front war: unprecedented Democratic enthusiasm and undeniable Republican apathy. - 🏈 President Trump's strategy is to whip up the MAGA faithful with rallies in the reddest parts of red states. - 😱 "The Red Scream is my biggest concern, not the blue wave," said Alex Castellanos, a veteran Republican consultant who has worked to help Trump get elected. - ‼️ "Republicans and independents are going to be screaming for attention, and many of them, including those who voted for Trump, may show their frustration by not showing up." Zoom in: Texas is starting to look like a late-season football showdown against an SEC rival: The GOP is still in the game, but defeat seems like a real possibility. - 🌾 In Kansas, Sen. Roger Marshall (R) has stopped the bleeding, but it's unclear whether there's enough time left to save his seat. - 🛥️ Republicans are quietly bullish on Michigan, but they recognize that the demographics have to break heavily in their favor, especially among Black voters. By the numbers: The math hasn't changed, but Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) sees multiple paths to 51 seats. - No one disputes that North Carolina is going to have a Democratic senator. It seems like another lifetime ago that Republicans were talking seriously about flipping Georgia. - If just two of the next tier of Ohio, Kansas and Alaska flip, the Senate would be split 50-50 before factoring in other competitive races, like Michigan, Iowa and Maine. 🦞 In Maine, Republicans and Democrats are consumed by competing fears. - Republicans are terrified that a national wave will be big enough to wash away Sen. Susan Collins. - Democrats, burned by her unforeseen survival six years ago, refuse to trust even the polls showing them ahead. 🎣 Between the lines: Maine and Alaska may be separated by more than 3,000 miles, but they pose a similar challenge for pollsters: small, overfished electorates where voters are increasingly unwilling to pick up the phone and bite on yet another survey. - Both could also see delays in their final results — potentially keeping the majority in limbo for days or weeks, as we told you last night.

Actor Walter Koenig, 'Star Trek's' plucky Chekov, dies at 90 Walter Koenig, who brought humor and grit to the role of starship navigator Pavel Chekov on the classic 1960s sci-fi TV series "Star Trek" and seven subsequent feature ‌films, has died at the age of 90. "My heart is heavy. Walter Koenig, our Ensign Pavel Chekov, passed away early today," George Takei, who starred alongside Koenig in the show and was a long-time friend, wrote on Facebook on Monday. US television ratings for the halftime performance often top 100 million viewers and ​rank higher than the audience for the game itself.
